description: We are Polaris Labs and we are reaching for the stars
summary: MAREKH is a crew walk planner for Mars, built on one real site: Home Plate in Columbia Hills, Gusev Crater. It turns HiRISE stereo terrain into a walkable three dimensional map, then answers the question a crew asks before a walk. What is the gentlest complete round trip inside a 500 metre budget, and where does it get steep? The app separates walking grade from ground slope, because crossing a slope at an angle changes the angle a person walks. It reports bounds instead of claiming an optimum. The saved route is 494.66 metres with a 2.6006 degree peak grade, and the grade floor is proven at 2.150 degrees. Three engines are selectable. One is a MER informed Field D planner with local crew steps. One is an A star baseline. One is a continuous planner that moves crossings inside native triangles. A separate Python and GDAL program audits both legs and sweeps crew clearance. A suited walk must return, so the decision needs evidence, not a picture.
details:
MAREKH is a crew walk planner for one documented site. Home Plate in Columbia Hills, Gusev Crater, is where the Spirit rover spent a winter. The app answers a question that orbital products leave open. What is the gentlest complete round trip inside a distance budget, and where does the route get steep?

The data layer merges an MRO HiRISE stereo terrain model with the matching HiRISE orthoimage. The terrain model sits at 1.011 metre posts on a 990 by 990 native grid. The app also carries a published Home Plate geologic map and reviewed exposure masks. The map is registered into that raster by masked normalized cross correlation, with a 0.4 pixel RMS fit. Every asset carries a SHA-256 hash from the source inventory, so a changed or truncated file is caught on load.

The app separates walking grade from ground slope. Walking grade is the angle along the direction of travel. Crossing a slope at an angle changes that angle, and the app reports the angle a crew would actually walk. The user picks a staging cell on the map, or types a native row and column. The user then asks for the gentlest walk inside a total distance budget, or the shortest walk under a peak grade cap.

Three engines are selectable. One follows the published MER architecture, with a Field D global cost field, short local crew steps and a one metre swept clearance. One is a plain A star baseline, kept for comparison. One is a continuous planner that searches elevation portals at 5 mm then 1 mm resolution. It then moves crossings continuously inside native triangles. A separate Python and GDAL program rechecks every finished route on both legs. It rebuilds roughness, sweeps the crew footprint, and re-measures geometry and grade from the raw heights. A failed check keeps the previous route.

Two design choices matter here. The search covers several spaces, not one. A grid A star and a Field D star cover the discrete surface. An elevation portal graph removes the eight direction limit. A convex solver then moves crossings continuously inside native triangles. A separate potential search proves a lower bound. So the app reports a bracket instead of an optimum. The saved route is 494.66 metres at a 2.6006 degree peak, with a proven floor of 2.150 degrees. No AI runs in the planner. The route is deterministic and reproducible, and an independent Python program re-audits it. Language model assistants helped write the code, the tests and the documentation, and the repository states this. We used AI to build the tool and kept it out of the decision.

Results are reported as bounds, not as an optimum. The saved route is 494.66 metres with a 2.6006 degree peak grade. A lower potential proves that no route can beat 2.150 degrees, so the grade bracket runs from 2.150 to 2.601 degrees. The distance bracket at that cap runs from 476.29 to 494.66 metres. The profile view scrubs with a distance cursor. It shows signed grade, crossed ground slope and surface warnings, and it jumps to the science turnaround or the next warning. Plans export as JSON and can be audited offline.

Benefits and impact. A crew planner can test a science target before anyone leaves the habitat. A geologist can see if an outcrop is walkable, not only visible. A mission team can trade distance against steepness and science payoff with numbers attached. The design favours evidence over a good looking line. Every claim in the app carries a hash, an audit or a stated bound.

Tools and languages. TypeScript, Bun, Vite, Three.js and Web Workers in the browser. Python 3.12 with GDAL, NumPy, SciPy and Clarabel for the continuous search and the independent checker. A C++17 solver drives the elevation portal search. The code is MIT licensed and runs from a single command.

Factors the team considered. A tight turn is crowded on Mars, so the app shows the cost of a gentler grade in metres, not only in degrees. Value comes from refusing false certainty, so the app shows the gap between the proven floor and the found route. The current data does not include temperature, radiation or walking time. The app shows those as unavailable instead of estimating them.
